prompt.context: Your client is Nutters of Savile Row, a legendary tailoring business that opened in 1969. At the height of its fame, Nutters dressed Mick Jagger, Twiggy, Elton John, and three of the four Beatles on the Abbey Road cover. Despite the departure of the two founders -- Tommy Nutter and Edward Sexton -- Nutters continues to have an excellent reputation. It offers customers made-to-measure and bespoke suits. Made-to-measure suits are cut, usually by machine, from an existing pattern and adjusted according to the customer's measurements. Bespoke suits are fully hand-made and the pattern is cut from scratch. Lately, however, Nutters has heard grumblings from customers. Fearing declining customer satisfaction, Alan Lewis, the current owner, has approached you for help.
prompt.question: What could be driving declining customer satisfaction at Nutters?

clarifying_info.q: What types of suits does Nutters offer?
clarifying_info.a: Made-to-measure and bespoke suits. Made-to-measure suits are cut from an existing pattern adjusted to customer measurements; bespoke suits are fully hand-made with the pattern cut from scratch.

clarifying_info.q: What data do we have on demand or order volumes?
clarifying_info.a: (Give Exhibit A if candidate asks about demand or order mix.)

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about Nutters's production process or capacity?
clarifying_info.a: (Give Exhibit B if candidate asks about production process or capacity.)

clarifying_info.q: What profit does each suit type generate?
clarifying_info.a: Made-to-measure suits generate $350 profit per suit; bespoke suits generate $900 profit per suit.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours does a full-time employee (FTE) work per month?
clarifying_info.a: One FTE works 160 hours per month.

clarifying_info.q: Should we assume demand is not a constraint when evaluating adding staff?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume demand is not a constraint -- if hiring Anson will produce more suits, there will be buyers for those suits.

exhibits.title: Orders Accepted
exhibits.shows: A table showing monthly orders accepted by suit type (made-to-measure and bespoke) and total, for February through May.

exhibits.title: Production Process
exhibits.shows: Two process flow diagrams: one for made-to-measure orders (at Beak Street workshop) and one for bespoke orders (at main Savile Row location). Each step shows time per order and FTE count. A footnote notes that for bespoke orders, the same 5 master tailors perform both patterning (step 2) and sewing (step 3).

framework: Quality: reputation/brand exclusivity, expertise of tailors, fit and attention to detail, feel of the space and service
Cost: price relative to customer expectations and relative to competitors
Speed: wait time at intake and delivery time (lead time from order to completion)
Flexibility: accessibility (hours, location), selection of styles/fabrics
Customer expectations: based on past experience, shop reputation, or competitors' offerings -- satisfaction is relative, not absolute

questions.prompt: Part 1 -- What could be driving declining customer satisfaction at Nutters?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify multiple dimensions of customer satisfaction (quality, cost, speed, flexibility). Strong answer notes that satisfaction is relative to expectations and that the high-end nature of the brand makes perceived quality and exclusivity important. Candidate should also hypothesize what has *changed* recently -- a weak answer says 'long wait times are inherent to artisan suits'; a strong answer says 'wait times have increased because demand spiked or capacity fell (e.g., lost staff).'

questions.prompt: Part 2 -- As it turns out, customers are unhappy with delivery time. Nutters has been experiencing increasing delays such that the percent of orders delivered on time has gone down. What might be causing the delay, and what data would you want?
questions.guidance: Let this be conversational -- gauge how well the candidate asks questions to obtain relevant data. If candidate mentions demand, give Exhibit A. If candidate mentions capacity or production process, give Exhibit B. From Exhibit A, candidate should observe that total orders are declining yet delays are increasing, pointing to the *mix* shift (more made-to-measure, fewer bespoke) as the driver rather than overall volume. From Exhibit B, candidate should calculate capacity at each step and identify the bottleneck. An excellent candidate also spots spare capacity in non-bottleneck steps and in the bespoke line.

math.setup: FTE works 160 hours/month. Capacity at each step = (160 hrs * FTEs) / (hours per order). The step with lowest capacity is the bottleneck and sets overall throughput.
steps: Made-to-measure -- Measuring: 160 hrs / 1 hr * 1 FTE = 160 orders/month
Made-to-measure -- Sewing: 160 hrs / 16 hrs * 5 FTE = 50 orders/month
Made-to-measure -- Finishing: 160 hrs / 4 hrs * 1 FTE = 40 orders/month
Bespoke -- Measuring: 160 hrs / 4 hrs * 1 FTE = 40 orders/month
Bespoke -- Patterning & Sewing combined (same 5 FTEs): 160 hrs / (14+18) hrs * 5 FTE = 160/32 * 5 = 25 orders/month
Bespoke -- Finishing: 160 hrs / 8 hrs * 2 FTE = 40 orders/month
Bespoke bottleneck = Patterning & Sewing at 25 orders/month
Conclusion: In April made-to-measure orders (42) exceeded the 40-order capacity; in May they reached 44 -- this excess caused the delays. Total system is not the issue; mix is.
math.answer: Made-to-measure max capacity = 40 orders/month; bespoke max capacity = 25 orders/month. Delays began when made-to-measure orders exceeded 40 in April (42) and May (44).

questions.prompt: Part 3 -- Nutters is considering hiring Anson, an experienced tailor who can do any step in either line. How much would you be willing to offer Anson and which step would you assign him to?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that max compensation = incremental profit Anson generates, which depends on where he is assigned. Key insight: adding Anson to a non-bottleneck step adds zero throughput because the bottleneck still limits output. Anson must go to the bottleneck step. Strong candidate recognizes that resolving one bottleneck may create a new bottleneck (e.g., fixing Finishing in made-to-measure reveals Sewing at 50 becomes binding). Strong candidate also weighs the tradeoff between profit ($4,500 bespoke vs $3,500 made-to-measure) and customer satisfaction (delay is in made-to-measure line).

math.setup: Incremental suits = new capacity at bottleneck step after adding Anson (1 additional FTE) minus old capacity. Salary cap = incremental suits * profit per suit.
steps: Option A -- Assign Anson to Finishing (made-to-measure bottleneck): new Finishing capacity = 160/4 * 2 FTE = 80 orders/month. But Sewing (50 orders) becomes the new bottleneck. Net gain = 50 - 40 = 10 more made-to-measure suits/month. Salary cap = 10 * $350 = $3,500/month.

Option B -- Assign Anson to Patterning & Sewing (bespoke bottleneck): new combined capacity = 160/32 * 6 FTE = 30 orders/month. Net gain = 30 - 25 = 5 more bespoke suits/month. Salary cap = 5 * $900 = $4,500/month.
math.answer: Option A salary cap: $3,500/month (adds 10 made-to-measure suits). Option B salary cap: $4,500/month (adds 5 bespoke suits). Bespoke assignment yields $1,000/month more in incremental profit.

brainstorming.prompt: Besides hiring Anson, what other ways could Nutters alleviate the delay problem?

categories.name: Capacity reallocation
ideas: Move FTEs from low-utilization steps (e.g., Measuring) to bottleneck steps if workers have the skills
Pool resources between made-to-measure and bespoke lines to avoid idle capacity in bespoke while made-to-measure is constrained

categories.name: Demand management
ideas: Cap or limit made-to-measure orders accepted per month to match capacity
Use waitlists or dynamic pricing to manage demand surges
Shift marketing emphasis toward bespoke suits (higher margin, more capacity headroom)

categories.name: Process improvement
ideas: Increase productivity per step through better tooling or workflow changes
Outsource lower-skill steps (e.g., finishing) to third parties during peak periods
Invest in technology to speed up made-to-measure cutting (e.g., automated cutting machines)

categories.name: Capacity expansion
ideas: Hire additional part-time tailors for bottleneck steps
Subcontract overflow orders to trusted partner tailors
Open additional workshop space to add parallel production lines

recommendation: Delays are caused by made-to-measure orders exceeding the shop's capacity of 40 orders/month, a situation driven by a shift in order mix toward made-to-measure as bespoke volume declines

To address the delay, assign Anson to either: (a) the Finishing step for made-to-measure, increasing effective throughput by 10 suits/month with salary cap $3,500/month, directly fixing the customer satisfaction problem; or (b) the Patterning & Sewing step for bespoke, increasing throughput by 5 suits/month with salary cap $4,500/month, generating $1,000 more incremental profit but not resolving the made-to-measure backlog

Given Nutters's brand equity and the client's stated concern about customer satisfaction, assigning Anson to made-to-measure Finishing is likely the better choice; the $1,000/month profit difference is modest relative to the reputational risk of continued delays
risks: Assigning Anson to Finishing (made-to-measure) merely shifts the bottleneck to Sewing (50 orders) -- if demand continues to grow, another hire will be needed
Waitlist or perceived exclusivity could be a brand asset; eliminating delays entirely may reduce perceived scarcity
Pooling resources across lines requires tailors to be cross-trained; bespoke master tailors may resist or lack skills for made-to-measure steps
next_steps: Assess whether current FTEs can be cross-trained or reassigned between steps to use spare capacity in Measuring
Evaluate whether made-to-measure and bespoke lines can share resources to eliminate idle capacity in bespoke during high made-to-measure demand periods
Monitor order mix monthly and set a capacity-based cap on made-to-measure orders accepted until throughput is increased
Consider strategic question of whether to grow made-to-measure volume or protect the bespoke brand positioning
